questions.q: What is the real conceptual difference between T-SQL's trigger model and Oracle's default trigger model?
options: T-SQL triggers are set-based (one firing per statement, holding many rows); Oracle FOR EACH ROW triggers fire once per individual row
T-SQL triggers can only fire on DELETE statements
Oracle triggers cannot access the changed data at all
There is no real difference — both fire exactly the same number of times
questions.explain: A 500-row T-SQL UPDATE fires its trigger once with all 500 row pairs in inserted/deleted; the same UPDATE fires an Oracle FOR EACH ROW trigger 500 separate times, once per row.

questions.q: How does Oracle's :NEW/:OLD syntax differ from MySQL's NEW/OLD?
options: Oracle's are colon-prefixed (:NEW, :OLD); MySQL's have no colon prefix (NEW, OLD)
They are spelled completely differently with no relation
MySQL uses colons and Oracle does not
Only one of the two platforms supports row-level references at all
questions.explain: Oracle references are colon-prefixed record references (:NEW.column), while MySQL drops the colon and references NEW.column directly.

questions.q: What makes PostgreSQL's trigger model structurally different from T-SQL's, Oracle's, and MySQL's?
options: PostgreSQL triggers are always two pieces: a separate trigger function containing the logic, plus a CREATE TRIGGER statement that just names when to fire it
PostgreSQL triggers cannot reference NEW or OLD at all
PostgreSQL has no concept of triggers
PostgreSQL triggers can only fire on SELECT statements
questions.explain: Unlike the other three platforms, which put the trigger's actual logic directly inside CREATE TRIGGER, PostgreSQL always calls out to a separately defined trigger function.

questions.q: What does FOR EACH ROW declare, and which platforms use it by default?
options: Row-level firing (once per affected row) — the default behavior in Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL
Set-based firing, used only by T-SQL
It has no effect on how often a trigger fires
It is exclusive to T-SQL's inserted/deleted tables
questions.explain: FOR EACH ROW declares row-level trigger execution, which Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL all use, in contrast to T-SQL's set-based model.

questions.q: For a single UPDATE statement that changes 10 rows, how many times does a T-SQL AFTER UPDATE trigger fire, compared to an Oracle FOR EACH ROW trigger on the same update?
options: T-SQL fires once (with all 10 rows available in inserted/deleted); Oracle fires 10 times, once per row
Both fire exactly once
Both fire exactly 10 times
T-SQL fires 10 times; Oracle fires once
questions.explain: T-SQL's set-based trigger model fires once per statement regardless of row count, while Oracle's default row-level model fires once per affected row.
